quests.instruction: Write N, O and P in a row. Each one starts at a different place, so check before you begin.
quests.question: N O P
quests.hint: N starts with a stem going down, O starts at the top and circles left, P starts with a stem and adds a bump.
quests.explanation: Three letters, three different first strokes. Choosing the first stroke before you write is how you stay in control.
quests.funFact: On the radio, N is spelled 'November', O is 'Oscar' and P is 'Papa', so spellings are clear even over a noisy line.

quests.instruction: Write Q, R and S in a row, keeping them the same size.
quests.question: Q R S
quests.hint: Q is a circle with a tail, R is a P with a leg, and S is a smooth double curve. Leave equal gaps.
quests.explanation: These letters use curves and tails. Make the extra parts, like the tail and the leg, small and clear.
quests.funFact: The 'three Rs' is an old way of saying that school teaches reading, writing and arithmetic.

quests.instruction: Write N through S in order, six letters in all.
quests.question: N O P Q R S
quests.correctAnswer: N O P Q R S
quests.hint: Take a breath before the row. Leave equal gaps and check that the tops line up after every two letters.
quests.explanation: Six letters mean six decisions about starting points. Keeping heights equal until the end is the challenge.
quests.funFact: On a compass, N means north and S means south.

quests.instruction: Write T, U and V in a row. Look out for the round bottom of U.
quests.question: T U V
quests.hint: T is bar and post, U has a curved bottom, V has a pointed one. Start each at the top line.
quests.explanation: Three letters that end in different ways: a post, a curve and a point. Finishing each stroke correctly is what keeps them clear.
quests.funFact: The letter T is the second most common letter in English writing, after E.

quests.instruction: Write W, X, Y and Z in order. These are the last four letters.
quests.question: W X Y Z
quests.hint: All four are slants. W has four, X has two crossing, Y has two meeting and a post, Z has two bars and one slant.
quests.explanation: Slanted letters need good control of direction. Check each slant matches the others in angle.
quests.funFact: X-rays got their name because the scientist who found them in 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen, did not know what they were and called them X.

quests.instruction: Write T to Z in order, all seven letters in a row.
quests.question: T U V W X Y Z
quests.correctAnswer: T U V W X Y Z
quests.hint: Plan the row: seven letters need narrow shapes and small gaps. Keep them on the line from start to end.
quests.explanation: Finishing the alphabet's last seven letters means you now have all 26 capitals in your hand.
quests.funFact: Old English used extra letters that we no longer use, such as thorn, which looked like Þ and stood for the 'th' sound.

quests.instruction: Write O and Q so that anyone can tell them apart.
quests.question: O Q
quests.hint: Make O a closed circle. Then write Q as a circle with a clear tail that crosses the bottom right.
quests.explanation: O and Q differ by only a tail, so the tail must be clear. That small detail is what makes a letter readable.
quests.funFact: In many computer fonts the letter O and the number zero are drawn a little differently, so they are not confused.

quests.instruction: Write M and W. One is the other turned upside down.
quests.question: M W
quests.hint: For M: pull down, slant down to the middle, slant up, pull down. For W: slant down, up, down, up. Make both the same width.
quests.explanation: W looks like M upside down, but you write it with different strokes. Knowing the strokes keeps each letter correct.
quests.funFact: W is the only letter in English whose name has three syllables: 'dou-ble-u'.

quests.instruction: Write V, Y and U in a row. Make each one clearly different.
quests.question: V Y U
quests.hint: V ends in a sharp point, Y has a stem, and U has a round bottom. Check each shape before you move on.
quests.explanation: Three similar open-topped shapes: telling them apart by the bottom part is useful for both writing and reading.
quests.funFact: Highway signs use big letters with wide spacing so drivers can read them from far away.

quests.instruction: Write C and G. Remember which one has the shelf.
quests.question: C G
quests.hint: Write C as an open curve. Write G the same way, but add a shelf in the middle pointing left.
quests.explanation: G is a C with an extra stroke. Without the shelf, the letters would be impossible to tell apart.
quests.funFact: The & sign was once a quick way to write the Latin word 'et', joining the letters e and t.

quests.instruction: Write H and N. Both have two stems, but they are joined in different ways.
quests.question: H N
quests.hint: H is joined by a bar across the middle, N is joined by a slant from top left to bottom right.
quests.explanation: Same stems, different connection. How strokes join each other is what makes letters unique.
quests.funFact: Chinese writing uses thousands of characters instead of a small alphabet.

quests.instruction: Write P, F and R in a row. Check the bumps and bars.
quests.question: P F R
quests.hint: P has a bump, F has two bars and no bump, R has a bump and a leg. Take your time with each.
quests.explanation: Practising confusing letters together makes your hand and memory focus on the small differences.
quests.funFact: In some English words, the letters 'ph' sound like F, as in 'phone'.

quests.instruction: Look at the letter S for five seconds, cover it, then write it from memory.
quests.question: S
quests.hint: Picture the path: curve left from the top right, swing across the middle, then curve right to the bottom left.
quests.explanation: Pulling a letter out of memory makes it stick better than copying again and again. If it looks off, take another look and try once more.
quests.funFact: Trying to remember something, instead of just looking at it again, is one of the best ways to learn.

quests.instruction: Look at K and W, cover them, and write both from memory.
quests.question: K W
quests.hint: Say what each one is made of: K is a stem plus two slants, W is four slants. Then write them.
quests.explanation: Describing the parts of a letter to yourself makes recall easier and your writing more confident.
quests.funFact: Some studies suggest that writing by hand can help people remember what they write.

quests.instruction: Look at B, G, Y and Z, cover them, and write all four in order from memory.
quests.question: B G Y Z
quests.hint: Break them up: B (stem and two bumps), G (C with a shelf), Y (two slants and a post), Z (bar, slant, bar).
quests.explanation: Four letters from memory is a real test. If one was hard, repeat it later; that is how memory grows.
quests.funFact: Ancient Egyptians used more than 700 different hieroglyph signs in their writing.

quests.instruction: Write T three times in a row. Make every T the same height and width.
quests.question: T T T
quests.hint: Write the first T, then use it as your model. Make the top bars the same length and the stems the same height.
quests.explanation: Repeating one letter shows how consistent you are. Your third letter should look like a twin of your first.
quests.funFact: The first pencils with erasers on the end were made in the 1850s.

quests.instruction: Write O three times. Keep them round and the same size.
quests.question: O O O
quests.hint: Start each at the top and go left. If one comes out wider, make the next one match the first.
quests.explanation: Round letters are easy to make too wide or too narrow. Comparing each to the first teaches your eyes to judge.
quests.funFact: A monospaced font gives every letter the same width, like the type on old typewriters.

quests.instruction: Write E three times, with the same bar lengths in each.
quests.question: E E E
quests.hint: Keep the middle bar a bit shorter than the top and bottom bars every time. Check all three letters.
quests.explanation: Bars the same length each time make letters look the same, even when you write them several times.
quests.funFact: No two people have exactly the same handwriting.

quests.instruction: Write the initials of Ravi Menon: the first letter of each name.
quests.question: R M
quests.hint: Use a capital letter for each initial. Leave a small gap between them.
quests.explanation: Initials are capital letters because names are special words. Writing the first letter of each name is a common use of capitals.
quests.funFact: The word 'initial' comes from the Latin word 'initium', which means 'beginning'.

quests.instruction: Write the initials of Anu Kumar Sharma, three names, three capitals.
quests.question: A K S
quests.hint: Write one capital for each name, keeping them the same size. A has a bar, K has slants, S has a double curve.
quests.explanation: Three initials in a row need even spacing and even size. This is real, useful handwriting.
quests.funFact: Some authors are known by initials, such as J. K. Rowling.

quests.instruction: Write the initials of Priya Jain Desai in order.
quests.question: P J D
quests.hint: P: stem and a bump. J: stem and hook. D: stem and a big curve. Space them evenly.
quests.explanation: Mixing stem letters and a hook letter makes you choose different strokes. Keep each one clearly shaped.
quests.funFact: A monogram is a design made from the initials of a person's name.

quests.instruction: Write STOP the way it appears on a sign, in capital letters.
quests.question: STOP
quests.hint: Write S, T, O, P in order. Keep the letters the same height and leave a small gap between each.
quests.explanation: Signs use capitals because they are easy to read from far away. Your letters need to be clear and evenly spaced.
quests.funFact: Stop signs have eight sides and are shaped like an octagon.

quests.instruction: Write EXIT in capital letters, like the sign over a door.
quests.question: EXIT
quests.hint: E has three bars, X is two crossing slants, I has small bars, and T has a bar and post. Space them equally.
quests.explanation: Four different shapes, one clear word. Spacing letters evenly makes the word easy to read at a glance.
quests.funFact: Exit signs are often lit so they can be seen even in the dark.

quests.instruction: Write OPEN in capital letters, like the sign on a shop door.
quests.question: OPEN
quests.hint: Start O at the top and circle left. P is stem and bump. E has three bars. N is two stems and a slant.
quests.explanation: A word is four letters with a rhythm: round, bump, bars, slant. Keep every letter on the baseline.
quests.funFact: In ancient Roman towns such as Pompeii, shops advertised with painted signs and symbols.

quests.instruction: Write H and I with a clear gap between them, about as wide as the letter I.
quests.question: H I
quests.hint: After H, stop and leave a space about as wide as a letter I before you start the next one.
quests.explanation: A good gap is neither too tight nor too wide. Letters that are too close may look joined together.
quests.funFact: Printers call the adjustment of space between two letters 'kerning'.

quests.instruction: Write A and V close together. Their slanted sides leave extra space, so tuck them in.
quests.question: A V
quests.hint: Write A, then start V slightly closer than normal, because the slants leave open air at the bottom.
quests.explanation: Slanted letters create empty space, so they can sit closer. Your eyes judge space by area, not by distance.
quests.funFact: Pairs such as AV are often moved closer by designers because their slanted sides leave a gap.

quests.instruction: Write W, A and Y in a row. Keep the spaces between them looking even.
quests.question: W A Y
quests.hint: Look at the spaces between the letters as shapes. Make them look equal, even if the distances are not exactly the same.
quests.explanation: Balancing the gaps in a row is the secret of neat handwriting. It gets easier with every row you write.
quests.funFact: Ancient Latin was often written with no spaces between words, which made it harder to read.

quests.instruction: From memory, write the first half of the alphabet: A to M.
quests.question: A B C D E F G H I J K L M
quests.correctAnswer: A B C D E F G H I J K L M
quests.hint: Say the letters in your head as you write. Plan the row so all thirteen fit with equal gaps.
quests.explanation: Thirteen letters in a row demands memory, control and spacing at once. It is a big step toward writing words.
quests.funFact: Alphabets are useful because a few dozen symbols can write every word in a language.

quests.instruction: From memory, write the second half of the alphabet: N to Z.
quests.question: N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z
quests.correctAnswer: N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z
quests.hint: Start with N and think of the last letters, W X Y Z, as slant letters. Keep every letter the same height.
quests.explanation: You now have all 26 capital letters. This is real hand control, built stroke by stroke.
quests.funFact: Before printing was invented, scribes copied books by hand, one letter at a time.

quests.instruction: Write the top row of letters on a keyboard: Q, W, E, R, T, Y.
quests.question: Q W E R T Y
quests.correctAnswer: Q W E R T Y
quests.hint: Don't write in alphabet order this time. Say the letters one by one, then write them with equal gaps.
quests.explanation: Letters out of order mean no pattern to lean on. Writing each from memory shows how strong your capitals are.
quests.funFact: The QWERTY layout was designed in the 1870s for an early typewriter made by Sholes and Glidden.
